title: Hooks for Course Creators: 36 Lines That Stop the Swipe
markdown:
# Hooks for Course Creators: 36 Lines That Stop the Swipe

At 0:02, a viewer decides whether your lesson is worth the next 28 seconds. If your video opens with “Today I’m going to talk about…,” they have already seen the pattern—and already have a thumb moving.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/uO68lfcXhM.png)

This page gives course creators ready-to-use opening lines for short videos, plus a simple way to choose one, test it, and turn it into a lesson that earns attention before it asks for it.

## Hooks for selling a course without leading with the course

Use these when the video should create recognition before you mention your offer.

1. “If you bought a course and never opened lesson two, this is probably why.”
2. “The problem is not that you need more discipline. It’s that your plan has no first move.”
3. “Before you enroll in another program, check whether you can answer this one question.”
4. “Most people try to learn this in the wrong order.”
5. “You do not need a longer to-do list. You need a decision rule.”
6. “Here’s the part of learning [TOPIC] that gets skipped—and then costs people weeks.”

## Hooks for teaching a beginner mistake

A useful beginner hook names the mistake without making the viewer feel foolish.

7. “You’re not behind. You started with the advanced version.”
8. “The first mistake in [TOPIC] happens before most people begin.”
9. “If this step feels confusing, do not push harder—check this first.”
10. “Beginners are told to do more. I’d start by removing this one thing.”
11. “Your first attempt at [TASK] should look almost too simple.”
12. “You do not need to master [TOPIC] today. You need to make this one choice correctly.”

## Hooks for a mini lesson or tutorial

Use a clear outcome when you can demonstrate the process quickly.

13. “Give me 30 seconds and I’ll show you how to turn [RAW MATERIAL] into [RESULT].”
14. “This is the three-step check I use before I publish [THING].”
15. “Here is the fastest way to find the weak point in your [PLAN/PROCESS].”
16. “Watch what changes when I replace this one sentence.”
17. “You can build your first [RESULT] with these three decisions.”
18. “Pause this video if you want the exact framework for [OUTCOME].”

## Hooks for a contrarian lesson

A contrarian hook needs a real correction behind it, not a louder opinion.

19. “Stop trying to be consistent before you make the work easier to repeat.”
20. “More information is not the answer to your [TOPIC] problem.”
21. “The popular advice on [TOPIC] misses the decision that matters first.”
22. “You do not need a niche before you make your first useful lesson.”
23. “A polished curriculum can be the reason nobody finishes it.”
24. “The best first lesson is often the one you are tempted to cut.”

## Hooks for proof, process, and behind-the-scenes videos

Show a real decision, screen, draft, or workflow after the line.

25. “This is what I check before I call a lesson ready.”
26. “I changed one part of this outline. Here is why the new version teaches faster.”
27. “This is the moment a vague course idea becomes a teachable promise.”
28. “Here’s how I turn one student question into a five-minute lesson.”
29. “I’m going to show you the before-and-after of a confusing explanation.”
30. “This is the template I use when a lesson has too much information.”

## Hooks for objections and hesitant buyers

Meet the objection directly, then deliver useful guidance whether or not the viewer buys.

31. “Think you do not have time for a course? Start with this 10-minute test.”
32. “If you are worried you will not finish, do not buy motivation—build a smaller start.”
33. “You do not need expensive tools to practice [TOPIC] this week.”
34. “If you have tried [METHOD] before and it did not stick, look at this step.”
35. “You can be a beginner and still make something useful before Friday.”
36. “Not sure whether [TOPIC] is for you? Try this one exercise before deciding.”

## Pick the hook that matches the video

Choose the opening based on what the viewer needs most in this specific clip.

- Use a **mistake** hook when they are doing something familiar but in the wrong sequence.
- Use a **question** hook when the viewer already feels a problem but cannot name it.
- Use a **demonstration** hook when the payoff can be shown on screen quickly.
- Use a **contrarian** hook when common advice is incomplete and you can explain the missing condition.
- Use an **objection** hook when hesitation is stopping a capable beginner from taking the next step.

The spoken line should make one promise. The next 5–10 seconds should prove that promise with a visual, an example, or the first step. If the hook says “three-step check,” show the check; do not spend the opening introducing yourself.

## Test hooks without guessing

Make two versions of the same short lesson. Keep the topic, footage, length, and call to action the same. Change only the first spoken line and the first on-screen text.

For example, test a question against a mistake:

- Version A: “Why does your course outline keep getting longer?”
- Version B: “Your course outline is getting longer because you skipped this decision.”

Review the recordings for a practical signal: which opening gets to the lesson fastest, sounds natural when spoken, and makes the next line feel inevitable? Keep the stronger direction, then test a more specific version of it. Replace vague words with the detail your audience recognizes: [ADD: their deadline], [ADD: their tool], or [ADD: their recurring problem].

## FAQ

### How long should a short-form hook be?

Long enough to create a clear reason to stay, short enough that the lesson starts immediately. Write the first sentence, say it aloud, and remove any word that does not change the promise.

### Should course creators use fear-based hooks?

Use stakes, not manufactured panic. “You are doing week one wrong” can lead to a helpful correction. A dramatic claim that the video cannot support breaks trust before the lesson begins.

### Can one hook work across TikTok, Reels, and Shorts?

The core idea can. Adapt the spoken pacing, on-screen text, and first visual to the clip you are making. The viewer still needs a concrete reason to stay in the first seconds.

### What should come after the hook?

Give the promised lesson: name the problem, show the method or example, and end with one next action. A hook is an opening agreement, not the whole script.

## What the tool returns

Here is a published example of the input and the shortened output:

**You send:** "Hooks for a 30s TikTok about why most people quit the gym in January — energetic, for beginners."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Positioning:** "The gym isn't the problem — your first week is." You own the beginner-who-keeps-quitting angle.
- **Hooks (5+, each with spoken line + on-screen text + type):**
  1. *Contrarian* — 🗣 "Stop going to the gym every day." / 🖥 "Day 1 is where you quit"
  2. *Question* — 🗣 "Why does everyone quit by January 20th?" / 🖥 "The January 20th wall"
  3. *Mistake* — 🗣 "You're not lazy. You're doing week one wrong." / 🖥 "Week 1 mistake"
- **Recommended pick:** #3, with one line on why it fits a beginner audience.
- **Script:** 0–3s hook · 3–10s the mistake · 10–22s the fix in 3 steps · 22–30s CTA.
- **Caption:** short caption + CTA + hashtags, plus one filming tip.
